newsitem.title: JORDAN: U.S. group calls for more press freedom in Jordan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. group calls for more press freedom in Jordan.

text.p: A U.S. journalists' group has called on King Hussein of Jordan to halt arrests of writers who criticise his government and to repeal a press law which it said directly threatened journalistic freedom.

The Committee to Protect Journalists listed seven Jordanian journalists either facing trial or appealing sentences on charges of insulting the king, publishing false or inaccurate news and libelling a member of parliament.
It said the charges against them had "contributed to a further deterioration of press freedoms in Jordan".

"We view their arrest and prosecution as clear violations of the right to freedom of expression," the organisation said in an open letter to King Hussein ahead of his talks with President Bill Clinton in Washington next Tuesday.

"These actions against press freedom call into question King Hussein's international image as a tolerant leader," CPJ executive director William Orme said in a statement faxed to Reuters with the letter.

The CPJ criticised Jordan's 1993 Press and Publications Law, which forbids journalists from publishing news which offends the king or the armed forces, reveals military information, contains contempt of religion, damages national unity, shakes confidence in the Jordanian dinar, insults officials of friendly nations, damages the dignity of an individual or violates public morals.

It said the law was "restrictive and vaguely-worded" and called on King Hussein to repeal articles "that directly threaten press freedom and contravene international human rights standards for a free press".

CPJ said journalists Nahed Hattar and Abdullah Abou Rouman face up to three years in jail on charges of lese-majeste, or insulting the king. Hattar was charged for articles including criticism of the permanent settlement of Palestinian refugees in Jordan and Jordan's diplomatic relations with Israel, CPJ said.
Abou Rouman's charges were based mainly on unpublished articles confiscated from his office which criticised bread price increases last August which led to rioting, it said.
Jordanian journalists said in January Abdullah bin Issa was sentenced to six months in jail for publishing an interview which a court said propagated an outlawed Islamist party doctrine.
Also in January two editors were sentenced to eight and nine month jail terms. One was additionally fined 15,000 dinars ($21,200) for "spreading false news and publishing pornographic material."
Journalists from the satirical Abed Rebbo are awaiting trial for labelling an Islamist member of parliament a hypocrite and accusing a former minister of corruption.
